text:
Recent work supports learning directional behavioral relationships rather than equating lexical similarity with next-item usefulness. [Collaboration and Transition (WSDM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.01056) builds a weighted, directed graph from item-transition frequencies and distills normalized transitions into a sequential recommender. [TGCL4SR (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28789) combines global temporal item-transition graphs with local sequences, using neighbor sampling, time perturbations and contrastive learning. Both offer mechanisms that do not require pretrained text models.

Complementarity research explicitly challenges similarity-only modeling. [TransGAT (ICDM 2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884336/) encodes behavioral direction, couples substitute and complement graphs, and uses self-supervised augmentation. [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) instead predicts complementary products through a directed, weighted projection of user–item interactions. These provide architectural ideas, but their relationship assumptions and supervision cannot automatically transfer to histories without substitute/complement labels. [SAGERec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/24/4844) integrates textual semantics with graph refinement, but requires LLM-derived embeddings, outside this task’s constraints.

A plausible adaptation—not an established result—is to combine training-only directed transitions with title/description token embeddings learned from scratch, using separate source and destination projections and an auxiliary next-item edge-prediction loss. Text could help generalize sparse transitions without forcing similar items together. Compare against transition-only and text-similarity-only ablations using macro validation HR@10. Treat discovered edges as predictive associations: histories alone do not establish substitution, complementarity, ownership, compatibility or unmet needs.
